cues.text: A Secret Christian in the Guard

According to the traditional Acts, Sebastian was born at Narbonne and raised in Milan, where St. Ambrose himself later attested to his veneration, and rose to become an officer in the Roman emperor Diocletian 's imperial bodyguard.
Unknown to the emperor he served, Sebastian was a devout Christian who used his position and access to quietly support and encourage persecuted believers throughout Rome.
Strengthening the Condemned

Tradition credits Sebastian with visiting Christian prisoners awaiting execution, most notably the twin brothers Mark and Marcellian, and bolstering their resolve to remain faithful even as their own families begged them to recant to save their lives.
His quiet ministry of encouragement reportedly won numerous converts among those who witnessed his conviction.
Discovered and Condemned
When Sebastian's Christianity was finally discovered — around 286, according to the Catholic Encyclopedia — the emperor felt personally betrayed by a trusted officer.
He ordered Sebastian bound to a stake in a field and shot by Mauritanian archers, his body left, in the vivid phrase later hagiographers used, 'as full of arrows as a hedgehog is full of spines.'
A Second Martyrdom
Left for dead, Sebastian was recovered by a Christian woman, traditionally named Irene , who discovered he was still breathing and nursed him back to health in secret.
Rather than flee Rome once recovered, Sebastian deliberately sought out Diocletian and confronted him publicly over his cruelty toward Christians.
This boldness so startled the emperor that, once he regained his composure, he ordered Sebastian beaten to death on the spot, a sentence this time carried out to completion.
Burial and Early Devotion
His body was thrown into Rome's sewer system but recovered by another Christian woman and buried along the Via Appia.
The fourth-century Depositio Martyrum already records his veneration there, providing early evidence for Sebastian's veneration in Rome.
Most narrative details, however, rest on later, legendary Acts rather than firsthand record.
Legacy: Patron Against Plague

Sebastian's association with archery and sudden, painful affliction later made him one of the most widely invoked saints against plague and pestilence across medieval and Renaissance Europe, and one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.

His dramatic double martyrdom — surviving arrows only to be clubbed to death — made him an especially popular subject for Renaissance painters including Botticelli, Mantegna, and Perugino, and he remains today the patron of soldiers, archers, and athletes.
